title: A word at the table (Avot 3:3)
hookLine: three who eat together and share no words of Torah have missed something holy

cards: Grease on the cardboard, the smell of oregano, a pile of napkins nobody will use. A pizza night is loud and good and over before the cheese cools. So what would make it holy?
Rabbi Shimon answers in Avot with a table. Three who eat at one table and say no words of Torah over it, he says, it's as if they ate from offerings to the dead.
But three who eat at one table and do say words of Torah, it's as if they ate from God's own table. Same food. Different table.

teach.h: THIS IS THE TABLE BEFORE THE LORD.
teach.b: Rabbi Shimon proves the good half from Ezekiel. In the prophet's vision of the Temple there's a wooden altar, and the angel says, "This is the table that is before the LORD."
The Mishnah hears it about any table where a word is shared. So a kitchen table can stand where an altar stood. Second, why three?
The Mishnah has another rule for that number. When three eat together, one invites the others to bless after the meal: an invitation called zimmun.
Three at a table is already a small congregation. Third, what counts as words of Torah?
Not a lecture. In some families a child gives a short dvar Torah at the Shabbat table, a word on the week's portion, a question, a line that stuck.
Saying the blessing after the meal counts too, some teachers say, since its words come from Torah. Fourth, the senses. A table isn't an idea.
It's wood under your forearms, a chair leg that wobbles, bread passed hand to hand, somebody's elbow in your space.
The Mishnah takes that whole ordinary scene and says: one good word, and you're eating somewhere holy. Nothing about the pizza has to change.

how: At Shabbat and holiday meals, some Jewish families share a short dvar Torah, and when three or more have eaten together, the grace after meals begins with a zimmun, an invitation to bless.

games.q: what does “a word at the table” mean?
o: one shared line of Torah that makes a meal holy
a blessing said before the first bite of bread
a polite rule against talking with your mouth full

games.q: around the table — tap the pairs.
p: three who eat at one table
the table that is before the LORD
the invitation to bless when three eat
a short word of teaching at a meal

s: the Mishnah calls a table with words of Torah the table of God
it quotes Ezekiel: this is the table that is before the LORD.
a word at the table has to be a long speech
a short dvar Torah, a question or a line will do; the Mishnah asks for words, not a lecture.
Jewish grace after meals has its own opening when three eat together
the Mishnah calls it zimmun, an invitation to bless.

games.q: family dinners at your place keep sliding into phones and complaints. by Rabbi Shimon's saying, what's the smallest change that counts?
o: one good word shared while everyone's still at the table.
a strict rule against talking at all during meals.
a long reading before anyone's allowed to eat.
games.why: the Mishnah doesn't change the food or the length of the meal. three at a table, one word of Torah between them, and it becomes God's table.

practice: Put both palms flat on a table, or whatever surface you eat at, and feel it: the grain, the cool, a crumb or two.
Breathe in whatever smell is near, then let one good line rise that you'd want said over that table, from this week or from anywhere. Keep your hands where they are until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: A word at the table: one line of Torah shared at a meal, which, Rabbi Shimon says, turns three people's dinner into God's table.

orig.note: Hebrew: the table of the Omnipresent, Avot 3:3.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: a word at the table, and the pizza can stay exactly as it is. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:3 (Rabbi Shimon: three who eat at one table)
